title: Sovereignty is a substrate

content_html:
There is a company in Japan that makes the seasoning in your instant ramen and the insulating film inside almost every advanced AI chip on the planet. It is the same company.

Ajinomoto is best known for inventing monosodium glutamate, a little pot of which lives next to my cooker. (My father-in-law mistook it for sugar and put two teaspoons of it in his tea once: I’m not sure he’s forgiven me yet.) Rather less well known than Ajinomoto’s fine work in seasonings is that a piece of chemistry that came out of that same materials research, Ajinomoto Build-up Film (ABF), turns out to be the dielectric layer that makes modern flip-chip substrates work. Every high-performance CPU and GPU sits on one. Ajinomoto controls something north of 95% of the film. (Compare and contrast with their better-known product: these days, Ajinomoto only actually makes 15%-20% of the world’s MSG.)

When people talk about who controls AI infrastructure, they’ll usually be thinking about Nvidia, or TSMC, or a hyperscaler with a datacentre the size of Liechtenstein. Almost none of them will have a food company in Kawasaki in mind.

They should. Because that is where the value in sovereignty is: not in the stuff that looks great in photos, or the stuff that gets all the breathless press interviews where CEOs catastrophise about AI bringing about the end of the world, but in the least glamorous, most concentrated link in the chain. It’s in the boring, infrastructure stuff that we don’t think twice about because it doesn’t occur to us to do so.

On 8 June, at London Tech Week, the government announced a £1.1 billion AI Hardware Plan. Liz Kendall called AI the “defining currency of economic and hard power” and said the countries that control the hardware will hold the keys to the future. She is right about that. But the mechanisms that are being put in place, on reading the plan closely enough to notice what it buys and what it doesn’t, don’t work.

The money breaks down roughly like this: £750 million for a national supercomputer landing in 2030, of which £400 million goes on next-generation chips. £150 million of that will be spent this summer, acting as an early customer for inference silicon (before the market gets an opportunity to decide who wins, which is another issue). There’s £120 million for an AI Hardware Innovation Programme to fund British firms to design, test and tape out novel chips. There’s up to £150 million from the British Business Bank to anchor a new fund (the BBB’s largest-ever commitment). And a skills package with a £12 million doctoral training centre in chip design and a partnership with Arm on top.

It is a serious, well-intentioned plan, and I do not want to be sniffy about public money going into hard technology for once; it’s a good thing. But look at the shape of it. This plan funds the two ends of the chain: the big compute at one end, chip design at the other; plus the people to do the design work. It is a plan built almost entirely around the layer Britain is already good at, which happens to be the layer that is most visible to someone who’s not a technologist, but who pays attention to the business pages. This is not a good thing.

Now read the whole plan again and look for the words packaging, substrate, test, or materials. They are not there. And having founded and worked at a company that designs and builds its own silicon, this is something I have spent the last fifteen years thinking very, very hard about.

A chip is not a thing you design and then own: there are a number of steps in between. A chip is a thing that gets designed, then fabricated, then packaged, then tested, and every one of those steps has its own map of organisations who can get in your way and make things grind to a halt.

Britain genuinely leads in design: look at Arm, and the long tail of talent around it. But design is the most portable layer in the entire stack. Arm’s whole business is the portability: it licenses an abstraction that anyone can implement on whatever process node is going. That is a wonderful thing to own if you are running a licensing company. It is also very nearly worthless as sovereignty, because the thing you own is the thing that travels most easily. My buddy Alasdair made a version of this argument about the Rekursiv last month: if you put the value above the silicon, it outlives any particular chip. There’s an uncomfortable corollary. Put the value above the silicon and it belongs to whoever can license it, from anywhere.

There is no leading-edge fab in Britain, and there is not going to be one. Any British-designed inference chip is fabbed by TSMC, just like everyone else’s. And TSMC’s fabs depend, in turn, on a lithography chain that is a monopolist’s fever dream: ASML for 100% of EUV machines, Carl Zeiss for 100% of the optics, TRUMPF as the sole supplier of the drive laser. There is a Japanese near-monopoly on the photoresist and a duopoly on the mask blanks. Not one of those links is British, and most are single points of failure for the entire world, not just the UK.

Nobody funds packaging, and everybody needs it. Taiwan does roughly 85% of advanced packaging; TSMC’s CoWoS capacity, the specific process that stitches an AI accelerator to its memory, is sold out and functions as the gate on how many AI chips exist right now. The dependency runs deep: the United States has committed something like $265 billion to onshoring fabs, and yet the US still flies the wafers out of its shiny new TSMC Arizona plant back to Taiwan to be packaged, because the packaging line isn’t there yet and won’t be until the end of the decade.

We don’t do substrate in the UK. Underneath the package sits the film we started with. A handful of licensees – Unimicron in Taiwan, Ibiden and Shinko in Japan, Nan Ya, and one European organisation, the Austrian firm AT&S – turn Ajinomoto’s ABF into substrates, and the top three hold about three-quarters of the market. In the 2021 shortage, lead times for some parts blew out past a year and companies as large as Broadcom ended up stuck in a queue. Ajinomoto has just put prices up 30%, effective this quarter, with the shortage forecast to run to the end of 2027, because there is nobody to buy from instead.

So this is what the geography of the British inference chips that the new government plan is paying to design and validate looks like. It’ll be designed in one of our two centres for ASIC design, Cambridge or Bristol. Fabbed in Taiwan on a machine only the Dutch can build. Packaged in Taiwan on a line only Taiwan runs at volume. Mounted on a substrate made from a film a noodle-seasoning company in Japan controls almost entirely.

Oriole Networks can build a brilliant optical interconnect to move data between those chips, but it still has to cross the planet twice before it becomes a thing you can switch on. The UK can win the layer the plan funds, comprehensively (although the funding’s probably not sufficient to do so – a matter for another article), and not move the sovereignty needle at all, because the sovereignty never captured a crucial part of the supply chain to start with.

None of this is a secret to anyone who has built silicon hardware or run a production line. The problem is always the one line on the bill of materials with a single supplier, a 30-week lead time, and a phone number in a time zone eight hours away from yours. A Raspberry Pi has hundreds of discrete components, from tiny surface-mounted electronics to functional silicon. If a single one of those is unavailable, all production stops dead. Sovereignty, at the scale of a country, is the same production line, but larger. The question is never “can we design it?” It is “who can stop us building it, and have we bothered to find out who they are?”

And this is why the current fashion for sovereignty frameworks is a bit beside the point. The EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package in June came with a four-level “assurance” scheme for cloud services; the Lords debated digital sovereignty on 23 July; Britain, characteristically, has no explicit sovereignty strategy at all and has muddled through on collaboration instead. Every one of these frameworks measures the visible stuff: where the data lives, whose cloud runs it, whether or not there’s a Union Flag fluttering bravely at the top of the flagpole on the datacentre. The dependency that would actually turn the lights out is way down the chain, in a build-up film from Japan, and none of the sovereignty frameworks so much as mention it.

At Negroni we look at manufacturing, silicon and hardware companies, and when we do, this is a big piece of the due diligence we run. Between your tape-out and a working system in a customer’s hands, how many pairs of hands touch the thing, and how many of them are a single company, in a single country, that could decide tomorrow you are no longer worth the trouble? If you cannot answer that, you do not have a supply chain. You have crossed fingers.

Kendall is right that the keys to the future are real. It’s just that a good few of them are held by a company better known for making MSG.

sentences.zh: 芯片是一种经过设计、制造、封装、测试的东西，每一个步骤都有自己的组织地图，这些组织可能会阻碍你并使事情陷入停滞。

blocks.html_en: Britain genuinely leads in design: look at Arm, and the long tail of talent around it. But design is the most portable layer in the entire stack. Arm’s whole business is the portability: it licenses an abstraction that anyone can implement on whatever process node is going. That is a wonderful thing to own if you are running a licensing company. It is also very nearly worthless as sovereignty, because the thing you own is the thing that travels most easily. My buddy Alasdair made a version of this argument about the Rekursiv last month: if you put the value above the silicon, it outlives any particular chip. There’s an uncomfortable corollary. Put the value above the silicon and it belongs to whoever can license it, from anywhere.

blocks.html_en: There is no leading-edge fab in Britain, and there is not going to be one. Any British-designed inference chip is fabbed by TSMC, just like everyone else’s. And TSMC’s fabs depend, in turn, on a lithography chain that is a monopolist’s fever dream: ASML for 100% of EUV machines, Carl Zeiss for 100% of the optics, TRUMPF as the sole supplier of the drive laser. There is a Japanese near-monopoly on the photoresist and a duopoly on the mask blanks. Not one of those links is British, and most are single points of failure for the entire world, not just the UK.

sentences.zh: 任何英国设计的推理芯片都是由台积电制造的，就像其他公司的一样。

blocks.html_en: Nobody funds packaging, and everybody needs it. Taiwan does roughly 85% of advanced packaging; TSMC’s CoWoS capacity, the specific process that stitches an AI accelerator to its memory, is sold out and functions as the gate on how many AI chips exist right now. The dependency runs deep: the United States has committed something like $265 billion to onshoring fabs, and yet the US still flies the wafers out of its shiny new TSMC Arizona plant back to Taiwan to be packaged, because the packaging line isn’t there yet and won’t be until the end of the decade.

blocks.html_en: We don’t do substrate in the UK. Underneath the package sits the film we started with. A handful of licensees – Unimicron in Taiwan, Ibiden and Shinko in Japan, Nan Ya, and one European organisation, the Austrian firm AT&S – turn Ajinomoto’s ABF into substrates, and the top three hold about three-quarters of the market. In the 2021 shortage, lead times for some parts blew out past a year and companies as large as Broadcom ended up stuck in a queue. Ajinomoto has just put prices up 30%, effective this quarter, with the shortage forecast to run to the end of 2027, because there is nobody to buy from instead.

Mounted on a substrate made from a film a noodle-seasoning company in Japan controls almost entirely.

blocks.html_en: None of this is a secret to anyone who has built silicon hardware or run a production line. The problem is always the one line on the bill of materials with a single supplier, a 30-week lead time, and a phone number in a time zone eight hours away from yours. A Raspberry Pi has hundreds of discrete components, from tiny surface-mounted electronics to functional silicon. If a single one of those is unavailable, all production stops dead. Sovereignty, at the scale of a country, is the same production line, but larger. The question is never “can we design it?” It is “who can stop us building it, and have we bothered to find out who they are?”

blocks.html_en: And this is why the current fashion for sovereignty frameworks is a bit beside the point. The EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package in June came with a four-level “assurance” scheme for cloud services; the Lords debated digital sovereignty on 23 July; Britain, characteristically, has no explicit sovereignty strategy at all and has muddled through on collaboration instead. Every one of these frameworks measures the visible stuff: where the data lives, whose cloud runs it, whether or not there’s a Union Flag fluttering bravely at the top of the flagpole on the datacentre. The dependency that would actually turn the lights out is way down the chain, in a build-up film from Japan, and none of the sovereignty frameworks so much as mention it.

blocks.html_en: At Negroni we look at manufacturing, silicon and hardware companies, and when we do, this is a big piece of the due diligence we run. content_html_zh:
日本有一家公司生产方便面的调味料和地球上几乎所有先进人工智能芯片内的绝缘膜。 这是同一家公司。

味之素因发明味精而闻名，我的炊具旁边就有一小锅。 （我的岳父把它误认为是糖，有一次在他的茶里放了两茶匙：我不确定他是否已经原谅我了。） 与味之素在调味品方面的出色工作相比，不太为人所知的是，味之素构建膜（ABF）是同一材料研究中产生的一种化学成分，它是使现代倒装芯片基板发挥作用的介电层。 每个高性能 CPU 和 GPU 都集成在一个上。 味之素控制着影片95%以上的部分。 （与他们更知名的产品进行比较和对比：如今，味之素实际上只生产了世界味精的 15%-20%。）

当人们谈论谁控制人工智能基础设施时，他们通常会想到英伟达、台积电或拥有列支敦士登大小数据中心的超大规模企业。 他们几乎没有人会想到在川崎开设一家食品公司。

他们应该。 因为这就是主权的价值所在：不是在照片中看起来很棒的东西，也不是在接受所有令人窒息的媒体采访时首席执行官们对人工智能带来世界末日的灾难性的东西，而是在链条中最不迷人、最集中的环节。 这是在无聊的基础设施方面，我们不会三思而后行，因为我们没有想到这样做。

6 月 8 日，在伦敦科技周上，政府宣布了一项 11 亿英镑的人工智能硬件计划。 莉兹·肯德尔 (Liz Kendall) 称人工智能是“经济和硬实力的定义货币”，并表示控制硬件的国家将掌握未来的钥匙。 她是对的。 但目前正在实施的机制，即仔细阅读该计划以注意到它购买了什么和不购买什么，并不起作用。

资金大致如下：7.5亿英镑用于2030年登陆的国家超级计算机，其中4亿英镑用于下一代芯片。其中 1.5 亿英镑将在今年夏天花费，作为推理芯片的早期客户（在市场有机会决定谁获胜之前，这是另一个问题）。 人工智能硬件创新计划拨款 1.2 亿英镑，资助英国公司设计、测试和流片新型芯片。 英国商业银行将提供高达 1.5 亿英镑的资金来设立新基金（BBB 有史以来最大的承诺）。 还有一个技能包，包括价值 1200 万英镑的芯片设计博士培训中心以及与 Arm 的合作伙伴关系。

这是一个严肃的、善意的计划，我不想对公共资金投入硬技术一次嗤之以鼻；这是一件好事。 但看看它的形状。 该计划为链条的两端提供资金：一端是大计算，另一端是芯片设计；加上做设计工作的人。 这是一个几乎完全围绕英国已经擅长的层面建立的计划，而这恰好是非技术专家但关注商业页面的人最容易看到的层面。 这不是什么好事。

现在再次阅读整个计划并查找“包装”、“基材”、“测试”或“材料”等字样。 他们不在那儿。 我创立了一家设计和制造自己的芯片的公司并在那里工作，这是我在过去十五年里一直在非常非常认真地思考的事情。

芯片不是您设计然后拥有的东西：其间有许多步骤。 芯片是一种经过设计、制造、封装、测试的东西，每一个步骤都有自己的组织地图，这些组织可能会阻碍你并使事情陷入停滞。

英国在设计方面真正处于领先地位：看看 Arm 以及围绕它的人才长尾。 但设计是整个堆栈中最可移植的层。 Arm 的全部业务就是可移植性：它授权任何人都可以在任何流程节点上实现的抽象。 如果您经营一家授权公司，那么拥有它是一件很棒的事情。 作为主权，它也几乎毫无价值，因为你拥有的东西是最容易移动的东西。 我的朋友 Alasdair 上个月就 Rekursiv 提出了这个论点的一个版本：如果你把价值放在硅之上，它就会比任何特定芯片的寿命都长。 有一个令人不安的推论。 将价值置于芯片之上，它就属于任何可以从任何地方获得许可的人。

英国没有、也不会有任何领先的晶圆厂。 任何英国设计的推理芯片都是由台积电制造的，就像其他公司的一样。 而台积电的晶圆厂反过来又依赖于垄断者狂热梦想的光刻链：ASML 提供 100% 的 EUV 机器，卡尔蔡司提供 100% 的光学器件，通快是驱动激光器的唯一供应商。 日本在光刻胶上近乎垄断，在掩模坯料上则形成双寡头垄断。 这些链接没有一个是英国的，而且大多数都是整个世界的单点故障，而不仅仅是英国。

没有人资助包装，但每个人都需要它。 台湾生产了大约 85% 的先进封装；台积电的 CoWoS 产能（将 AI 加速器缝合到内存的特定工艺）已售罄，并且充当着目前存在多少 AI 芯片的大门。 这种依赖性根深蒂固：美国已承诺向境内晶圆厂投入约 2650 亿美元，但美国仍然将晶圆从其闪亮的新台积电亚利桑那工厂运回台湾进行包装，因为包装线尚未建成，而且要到本世纪末才会建成。

我们在英国不生产基材。 包裹下面放着我们开始看的电影。 台湾的欣兴微电子、日本的 Ibiden 和 Shinko、Nan Ya 以及一家欧洲组织奥地利公司 AT&S 等少数被许可方将味之素的 ABF 制成基板，前三名占据了约四分之三的市场份额。 在 2021 年的短缺中，一些零件的交货时间超过了一年，像博通这样大的公司最终陷入了排队。 味之素刚刚将价格上涨 30%，本季度生效，预计短缺将持续到 2027 年底，因为没有人可以替代。

这就是新政府计划付费设计和验证的英国推理芯片的地理位置。 它将在我们的两个 ASIC 设计中心之一（剑桥或布里斯托尔）进行设计。 在台湾用只有荷兰人才能制造的机器制造。 在台湾包装，只有台湾的生产线才能批量生产。 安装在由薄膜制成的基板上，日本一家面条调味公司几乎完全控制着它。

Oriole Networks 可以构建出色的光学互连来在这些芯片之间传输数据，但它仍然需要穿越地球两次才能成为可以打开的东西。 英国可以全面赢得该计划资助的层面（尽管资金可能不足以做到这一点——这是另一篇文章的问题），并且根本不会移动主权针，因为主权从未占据供应链的关键部分。

对于任何构建过硅硬件或运行生产线的人来说，这都不是秘密。 问题始终出在物料清单上的一行，只有一家供应商、30 周的交货期以及与您所在时区相距 8 小时的电话号码。 Raspberry Pi 具有数百个分立组件，从微型表面安装电子设备到功能硅。 如果其中一个不可用，所有生产都会停止。 主权，在一个国家的规模上，是同一条生产线，但规模更大。 问题从来不是“我们能设计它吗？” 问题是“谁能阻止我们建造它，我们有没有费心找出他们是谁？”

这就是为什么当前流行的主权框架有点离题。 欧盟六月份的技术主权一揽子计划为云服务提供了四级“保证”计划；上议院于 7 月 23 日就数字主权展开辩论；英国的特点是，根本没有明确的主权战略，反而在合作方面蒙混过关。 这些框架中的每一个都测量可见的东西：数据存储在哪里，谁的云运行它，数据中心旗杆顶部是否有一面英勇飘扬的英国国旗。 在一部来自日本的电影中，实际上会关灯的依赖关系是在链条的下游，而没有一个主权框架提及它。

在内格罗尼，我们会关注制造、芯片和硬件公司，当我们这样做时，这是我们进行尽职调查的重要组成部分。 在你的流片和客户手中的工作系统之间，有多少双手接触这个东西，其中有多少双手是在一个国家的一家公司，这可能决定明天你不再值得麻烦？ 如果你不能回答这个问题，那么你就没有供应链。 你已经交叉手指了。

肯德尔说得对，未来的钥匙是真实的。 只是其中有相当一部分是由一家以生产味精而闻名的公司持有的。
